statement: \textnormal{Let f range over nonnegative measurable real functions with the stated finite nonzero squared integral. Find the ordered pair consisting of the smallest constant C valid for every such f and yes or no to whether equality holds for any such f.}\quad0<\int_0^\infty f(x)^2\,\mathrm dx<\infty,\qquad\int_0^\infty\int_0^\infty \frac{(xy)^{\frac{11}{4}}}{(x+y)^{\frac{13}{2}}}f(x)f(y)\,\mathrm dx\,\mathrm dy\le C\int_0^\infty f(x)^2\,\mathrm dx.\quad\Gamma(z)=\int_0^\infty t^{z-1}e^{-t}\,\mathrm dt\quad(z>0).

choices.misconception: Treat the nonintegrable constant in logarithmic coordinates as an admissible extremizer
Combine the kernel normalization and attainment mistakes

steps: \textnormal{Denote the double integral in the question by J. Define the Gamma function used below.}
\textnormal{Use logarithmic coordinates to expose the scale invariance. Define the positive shape parameter and the isometric change of unknown.}
p=\frac{13}{2},\quad x=e^u,\quad g(u)=e^{u/2}f(e^u),\qquad\int_0^\infty f(x)^2\,\mathrm dx=\int_{\mathbb R}g(u)^2\,\mathrm du.
\textnormal{All original factors, including both Jacobians, combine into a kernel depending only on the difference of the logarithmic coordinates.}
k_p(t)=(2\cosh(t/2))^{-p}>0,\qquad J(f)=\int_{\mathbb R}k_p(t)\left(\int_{\mathbb R}g(u)g(u-t)\,\mathrm du\right)\mathrm dt.
\textnormal{Translation preserves the squared integral. Cauchy–Schwarz bounds each inner correlation by that integral. Tonelli applies because the functions and kernel are nonnegative.}
J(f)\le C_p\int_{\mathbb R}g(u)^2\,\mathrm du,\qquad C_p=\int_{\mathbb R}k_p(t)\,\mathrm dt.
\textnormal{With the exponential substitution, the kernel mass is an Euler beta integral. Both endpoints converge because the shape parameter is positive.}
\textnormal{To prove this constant cannot be lowered, use normalized indicators of longer and longer intervals in logarithmic coordinates.}
\textnormal{Dominated convergence applies with the integrable kernel as majorant. These are admissible nonzero functions for every positive L, so the bound is sharp.}
\textnormal{Finally, equality would make every translation defect vanish for almost every shift. The following nonnegative identity makes the obstruction explicit.}
C_p\int_{\mathbb R}g^2-J(f)=\frac12\int_{\mathbb R}k_p(t)\int_{\mathbb R}(g(u)-g(u-t))^2\,\mathrm du\,\mathrm dt.

\textnormal{Translations are continuous in the L2 norm. Since the kernel is strictly positive, equality forces translation invariance for every shift. A translation-invariant L2 function on the real line is constant almost everywhere, and the only such square-integrable constant is zero. This contradicts the required nonzero squared integral.}

\textnormal{Consequently the smaller of their magnitudes tends to zero. Therefore }\limsup f\le\frac12\max\{1,2\}.
